Thanks for the ping — quick ops notes (summary, followed by suggested redline language):

Summary:
- P1 acknowledgement 30 min is OK (we can auto-acknowledge incident receipts), but a 4-hour remediation "commitment" is risky given varied root causes (hardware, model regression, 3rd-party infra). We can commit to mean-time-to-first-action and a workaround SLA for hosted customers and stronger on Dedicated.
- Blackout handling: 14 days notice for non-emergency planned maintenance is fine. For rolling upgrades / urgent security patches, we need the right to perform emergency maintenance with best-effort notice plus a post-facto report.
- Credit formula: we generally start credits at <99.9% for production endpoints. Their ladder starting at 99.7% will materially raise liability. Recommend a capped credit approach and exclusion for scheduled maintenance and customer-induced outages.

Suggested redline snippets (for Laura to convert to tracked changes):
- Replace "Customer may request blackout dates" with "Customer may request blackout dates in writing; Redwood will use commercially reasonable efforts to accommodate such requests for no more than 2 blackout weeks per 12-month period for Hosted deployments. For Dedicated deployments, blackout accommodations will be handled per the Dedicated support schedule."
- For emergency maintenance: "Redwood may perform emergency maintenance to address security or stability vulnerabilities; Redwood will provide notice as soon as practicable and a post-maintenance report."
- Credit ladder: "Service credits apply when Monthly Uptime Percentage for a given Service falls below 99.9% (as defined). Credits are capped at a % of monthly fees and exclude scheduled maintenance and force majeure events."

Attachment: redline_sla_recommendation_avery_v1.docx (docx) — contains proposed wording and example credit math.

If you want, I can mock a table showing cost impact for them if credits kick in under multiple scenarios — might help procurement understand trade-offs.

- Aditya
Head of Platform Reliability | Redwood Inference
aditya_rao@redwood.com

Thanks, team — I reviewed ClearPort's pdf and Aditya's proposed snippets. A few legal points and next steps:

Legal edits:
1) Blackout requests: convert to a formal "Blackout Request" workflow. We will accept up to two blackout weeks per 12-month period for Hosted; customer must submit requests 21 days in advance to enable operational planning. (21 days gives us runway across regions.)
2) Emergency maintenance carveout: add a requirement that Redwood must provide a post-event report within 72 hours for emergency maintenance that impacts uptime.
3) P1 language: change "4-hour remediation commitment" to "4-hour initial response and engagement; remediation time will vary based on incident class and root cause. Redwood will provide status updates every 4 hours until resolution or workaround."
4) Credits: add a dollar cap tied to monthly recurring charges (e.g., credits may not exceed 50% of monthly fees) and state that credits are Redwood's sole and exclusive remedy for availability issues.

Next steps: I'll produce a single tracked-changes Order Form that incorporates Aditya's operational notes and legal language. Avery, please confirm we can send the tracked-change file to Maya and whether you want to propose a 2-week feedback window.

--
Laura Bennett

Avery / Laura / Aditya — thanks for the quick review and proposed language. A few clarifications from ClearPort: 
- 21 days notice works for planned maintenance; procurement will try to limit blackout requests to end-of-quarter days only.
- For P1: procurement will accept the 4-hour initial response + engagement model provided Redwood adds a clause committing to a post-incident RCA for P1 incidents within 10 business days.
- Credits: procurement accepts a capped credit approach, but requests that the monthly cap be at least 75% of the monthly fee for the first 12 months of the relationship (they argue for an introductory ramp).

We attached a short counterproposal for your tracked changes and a redline PDF showing the specific clauses we would like retained or moved.
